lead: Real gas streams carry several solutes, and one solvent must remove all of them. Each solute has its own Henry constant and its own equilibrium line, but the liquid and gas flow together, so one L/G serves every component. A reactive solvent goes further: the dissolved solute is consumed by a chemical reaction, so the liquid film can hold far more and the absorption rate rises by an enhancement factor. These ideas set the solvent choice and column size for CO2 or H2S removal with amines, SO2 scrubbing with lime, and many gas-cleaning plants.
prereq: You need: Henry's law, equilibrium and operating lines, absorption factor, and HTU/NTU; film theory from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A multicomponent absorber receives a gas with solutes A, B, C and one liquid. At equilibrium each solute obeys its own Henry law: y<sub>i</sub> = m<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub>, where y<sub>i</sub> is mole fraction in the gas, x<sub>i</sub> is mole fraction in the liquid, and m<sub>i</sub> is the slope of that solute's equilibrium line. One m per solute, not one average m for the mixture.

The operating line is shared. A solute balance gives the same liquid flow L and gas flow G for every component, so L/G is one number. For component i the absorption factor is A<sub>i</sub> = L/(m<sub>i</sub>G). It is dimensionless. Large A<sub>i</sub> means easy absorption; small A<sub>i</sub> means hard absorption.

Find the key component first. Compute A<sub>i</sub> for each solute. The component with the smallest A<sub>i</sub> is hardest to absorb and usually needs the most stages; it fixes L/G and the stage count. Then apply the Kremser equation component by component, using each solute's own A<sub>i</sub> and its own inlet and outlet mole ratios. Some syllabi call the shortcut group method the Edmister method; it handles several components together by grouping. Never replace the individual m<sub>i</sub> values by an average Henry constant.

A reactive solvent removes solute by reaction as it dissolves. Common examples are CO2 in NaOH or amine, H2S in amine, and SO2 in lime slurry. The reaction keeps dissolved solute concentration low, so more gas can dissolve. Film and penetration models with reaction compare reaction rate with diffusion rate; that comparison gives the Hatta number.

blocks.where: k is the pseudo-first-order reaction rate constant (s⁻¹); D<sub>A</sub> is the solute diffusivity (m²/s); k<sub>L</sub> is the liquid-film mass transfer coefficient (m/s). Ha is dimensionless.

blocks.text: The enhancement factor E is the flux with reaction divided by the flux without reaction at the same interfacial concentration. Its size depends on Ha.

items: Slow reaction, Ha below about 0.3: reaction occurs mainly in the bulk liquid, E ≈ 1, and the rate is close to physical absorption.

Fast reaction, Ha above about 3 and much smaller than E<sub>i</sub>: reaction occurs inside the film and E ≈ Ha, so the flux is multiplied by Ha. E<sub>i</sub> is the instantaneous enhancement factor defined in the next bullet.

Instantaneous reaction: the reaction plane is sharp. When Ha is comparable to or larger than E<sub>i</sub>, use E = E<sub>i</sub> = 1 + D<sub>L</sub> c<sub>B</sub> / (b D<sub>A</sub> c<sub>Ai</sub>), where D<sub>L</sub> is diffusivity of liquid reactant B (m²/s), c<sub>B</sub> is its bulk concentration (kmol/m³), b is the stoichiometric coefficient of B per mole of A, D<sub>A</sub> is solute diffusivity (m²/s), and c<sub>Ai</sub> is interfacial solute concentration (kmol/m³).

blocks.text: Consequences: solvent capacity rises, so the liquid rate falls; the back pressure of solute is nearly zero, so the equilibrium gas mole fraction is y<sup>*</sup> ≈ 0; the driving force is y − y<sup>*</sup> ≈ y; the liquid-film resistance shrinks and the gas film may control. In the figure, the fast-reaction curve is the approximation exp(−Ha x/δ) with Ha = 3; for a finite film with zero bulk solute, the exact first-order profile is c<sub>A</sub>/c<sub>Ai</sub> = sinh[Ha(1 − x/δ)]/sinh(Ha), which is zero at the film edge x/δ = 1.

For a fast reaction with y* ≈ 0, the driving force y − y* ≈ y, so the operating line has almost the full gas mole fraction as driving force. The NTU and HTU method from Chapter 3.7 still applies, but if the liquid film resistance disappears, the overall gas coefficient is close to the gas-film coefficient. The tower becomes gas-film controlled, so packing wetting and gas velocity matter more than liquid-side kinetics.

Multicomponent plus reaction means each solute has its own m<sub>i</sub>, Ha<sub>i</sub>, and E<sub>i</sub>. A reactive solvent may remove H2S fast and CO2 slowly; selectivity then comes from kinetics, not only solubility. The key component can change, so solve each component's flux with its own E<sub>i</sub> and then satisfy the single L/G. Check the gas film before reducing the liquid rate too far.

figure.caption: The straight line is physical absorption. With Ha = 3 the fast-reaction curve is the semi-infinite approximation exp(−Ha x/δ): the solute is consumed inside the film. The exact finite-film first-order profile is sinh[Ha(1 − x/δ)]/sinh(Ha), which reaches zero at the film edge.

spec.aria: Concentration of dissolved solute across the liquid film falls linearly without reaction and falls steeply near the interface when a fast reaction consumes the solute inside the film.

examples.question: CO2 is absorbed into a solution in which it reacts with a pseudo-first-order rate constant k = 100 s⁻¹. The CO2 diffusivity is D_A = 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, the liquid film coefficient is k_L = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, and the interfacial concentration is c_Ai = 0.03 kmol/m³. Find Ha, the enhancement factor, and the absorption flux. Compare with physical absorption.
steps: Write the data: k = 100 s⁻¹, D_A = 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, k_L = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, c_Ai = 0.03 kmol/m³.
Ha = 20 is well above 3, so the reaction is fast and E ≈ Ha = 20.
Flux with reaction = E k_L c_Ai = 20 × 2 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.03 = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ kmol/(m²·s).
examples.answer: Ha = 20, E ≈ 20, and the reactive flux is 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ kmol/(m²·s), twenty times the physical flux of 6 × 10⁻⁷ kmol/(m²·s).
examples.check:
k = 100.0
D = 1.6e-9
kL = 2e-5
cAi = 0.03
Ha = (k * D) ** 0.5 / kL
E = Ha
flux = E * kL * cAi
physical = kL * cAi
ratio = flux / physical
print(Ha)
print(E)
print(flux)
print(physical)
print(ratio)

traps: Using one average Henry constant for a mixture. Each solute has its own m<sub>i</sub>, so each has its own equilibrium line.
Setting a separate L/G for each solute. One liquid and one gas flow serve every component; the key component fixes the shared L/G.

Applying E = Ha outside the fast-reaction range. E ≈ Ha is valid only when Ha is above about 3 and much smaller than E<sub>i</sub>; for slow reaction E is near 1, and when Ha is comparable to or larger than E<sub>i</sub> use E = E<sub>i</sub>.
Mixing units in Ha: k must be in s⁻¹ for pseudo-first-order reaction, D<sub>A</sub> in m²/s, and k<sub>L</sub> in m/s.
Treating the instantaneous-reaction formula as general. It applies only when the reaction is extremely fast and reactant B is present in the liquid.

quiz.q: Define the enhancement factor E in absorption with chemical reaction.
quiz.a: E = flux with reaction divided by flux without reaction at the same interfacial concentration and liquid flow. It is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why is L/G a single value in a multicomponent absorber?
quiz.a: All solutes share the same liquid and gas streams. A solute balance gives one L and one G, so L/G is fixed for the column; only m_i and A_i differ from solute to solute.

quiz.q: For k = 50 s⁻¹, D_A = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, and k_L = 3 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, find Ha.
A reacting system gives Ha = 0.5. Explain whether E ≈ Ha is a good estimate.
quiz.a: No. Ha = 0.5 is not in the fast-reaction range. E ≈ Ha needs Ha above about 3. At 0.5 the reaction is largely in the bulk liquid and E is closer to 1; using 0.5 would understate the flux.

quiz.q: For an instantaneous reaction, D_L = D_A, b = 1, c_B = 0.1 kmol/m³, and c_Ai = 0.02 kmol/m³. Find E.
Explain two design consequences of a fast reaction with E much greater than 1.
quiz.a: Solvent capacity rises, so the liquid rate can fall. The equilibrium back pressure is nearly zero, so y<sup>*</sup> ≈ 0 and the driving force is y − y<sup>*</sup> ≈ y. Liquid-film resistance shrinks, so the gas film may control and the tower becomes gas-film controlled.

quiz.q: Name the shortcut group method used for multicomponent absorption.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial CO2 capture with amine solvents is a reactive absorber where the Hatta number and enhancement factor decide the packing height. Rate-based simulators solve the film equations with reaction instead of using a single E. Rotating packed beds and ionic liquids are newer ways to raise solvent capacity. Search next for "Hatta number", "enhancement factor", and "rate-based absorption". Only a few universities teach this chapter in detail; most stop at the Hatta number.
